entries.clue: Hold together, split apart (6)

blocks.note: the older sense, to stick fast to a person or a principle, as the marriage service has it
the butcher's sense, to chop a carcass right through

annotation.surface: An instruction to hold something together and then break it in two.
annotation.walkthrough: Two Old English verbs, clifian 'to stick' and cleofan 'to split', wore down into the same six letters, so the clue can flatly contradict itself and stay accurate. A word that is its own opposite is a contronym.
annotation.definitionFit: Holding together is the clinging sense the marriage service uses; splitting apart is what the butcher's blade does, and English keeps both under one spelling.

entries.clue: Move with difficulty to raise either end of rear in this altered tartan item (10,5)

indicatorNotes.either end of: Whichever end of the word you choose, it is the same letter, so one letter comes away from it.
indicatorNotes.altered: What has been altered is no longer as it was, so the letters gathered before it are rebuilt in a new order.

blocks.note: to lumber is to move heavily and awkwardly, the way a bear does
to jack a car is to raise it off the ground
rear opens and closes on the same letter, so either end hands over R
the little word itself, four letters to be shuffled in with the R

annotation.surface: Shifting awkwardly to hoist the back end of a made-over tartan garment.
annotation.walkthrough: A lumberjack shirt is the heavy checked flannel one worn by woodsmen, and its bold check passes for tartan. 'Rear' hands over one letter rather than two, because both its ends are the same.
annotation.definitionFit: Tartan is the Scottish checked cloth, and the red-and-black check of a woodsman's shirt is close enough that the garment is sold as tartan.

entries.clue: As spelled out in full, one of Agatha’s poisons (7)

indicatorNotes.spelled out in full: Spelling a short form out in full replaces it with the whole word it stands for, so two letters become the name they abbreviate.

blocks.note: As is the periodic table's symbol for element 33, and the symbol written out at full length is its name

annotation.surface: One of the poisons Agatha reached for, given its full name.
annotation.walkthrough: Agatha is Christie, who trained as a dispenser in a hospital pharmacy and poisoned more characters than any other novelist. The clue trusts you to read 'As' as a chemical symbol rather than as the little word it looks like.
annotation.definitionFit: Christie's plots turn on poison more than any other device, and this element is among the ones she used repeatedly, so she can name it by association.

entries.clue: States’ fast trains (9)

blocks.note: to state a view is to put it into words
the services that run between the big stations without stopping at the little ones

annotation.surface: The high-speed railway services of the American states.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the disguise: it turns the first word into a possessive, so the clue reads as railways belonging to the States when that word is a verb standing on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who states an opinion expresses it, and the trains that skip the small stops are expresses, so the plural -s serves both halves.

entries.clue: Prudent having tamed mammal before start of December (6)

indicatorNotes.before: What stands before another thing goes in front of it, so the mammal's letters lead and the single letter follows.
indicatorNotes.start of: The start of a word is the letter it opens on, so only that one letter is taken from the month.

blocks.note: the small sharp-nosed insect-eater of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew
the opening letter of the month

annotation.surface: A careful person who has tamed a small animal by the beginning of December.
annotation.walkthrough: The mammal arrives by way of Shakespeare, whose play is about taming one, which is why the adjective is doing the pointing. A shrew is a mouse-sized insect-eater with a long pointed snout.
annotation.definitionFit: Prudent and shrewd both describe judgement that sees what is coming, the second leaning towards sharp practical canniness rather than caution.

entries.clue: Principally, such provision only requires knife! (5)

annotation.definition: Principally, such provision only requires knife!

indicatorNotes.Principally: What is done principally is done first of all, so every word gives up the letter it begins on and nothing more.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the determiner
the letter this noun begins with
the front letter of the adverb
the initial of the verb
the opening letter of the last word

annotation.surface: A table laid so meanly that the one thing still wanted is a knife.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing is left over to serve as a separate definition: the sentence spells the word and describes it at once. A spork is a spoon with a fork's prongs cut into its bowl, and cutting is the one job it cannot do.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue says what the thing is: lay one of these and the only other implement the diner still needs is a knife.

entries.clue: Banal comedian’s material (7)

blocks.note: dull because it is the same every time
the run of gags a stand-up works through on stage

annotation.surface: A comedian whose act is dull stuff.
annotation.walkthrough: The join falls after the first word and nothing marks it, so the two definitions read as one insult. Both senses come from the same idea of a fixed round gone through again and again.
annotation.definitionFit: Anything banal is dull through repetition, and a stand-up's act is a fixed sequence performed night after night, so one word covers both.

entries.clue: Surgery query: ‘How red is he?’ … utter jerks (5,4,2,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is the question itself rather than a synonym for a query: the setter names the words by the room they are asked in.

indicatorNotes.jerks: A jerk is a sudden yank, and letters yanked about do not come to rest in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
five more letters of the fodder, joined on to the quoted question
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone at the doctor's asking how red the patient has gone, then writing off a pair of idiots.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an instruction to say something aloud and is five of the fifteen letters instead. In Britain a surgery is the room where a GP sees patients, not an operating theatre.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the doctor's first question to a patient in pain, so naming the room is enough to identify the phrase said in it.

entries.clue: Make huge amounts of faulty damp-courses (4-7)

indicatorNotes.faulty: Something faulty has gone wrong in the making, so its letters have not come out in the order they should.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A builder turning out damp courses that are not up to the job.
annotation.walkthrough: A damp course is the waterproof layer built into a British wall a brick or two above the ground to stop damp rising, which is why the surface sounds like a complaint about shoddy building.
annotation.definitionFit: To mass-produce is to turn something out in bulk on a production line, which is making it in huge amounts by machine rather than by hand.

entries.clue: Regularly avoided collision reversing in capital city (4)

indicatorNotes.Regularly avoided: Letters avoided at a regular interval are the ones left out, so the word hands over only every second letter.
indicatorNotes.reversing: Something reversing runs back along its own path, so the letters collected are read the other way round.

blocks.note: skipping the odd letters of collision — c, l, i, i, n — leaves o, l, s, o

annotation.surface: A driver who regularly avoids a collision while reversing in a capital city.
annotation.walkthrough: Oslo is Norway's capital, at the head of its fjord. 'Reversing' does double duty in the surface as what the car is doing, which covers its job as an instruction to the solver.
annotation.definitionFit: Oslo is Norway's seat of government and its largest city, so the definition names it by the office it holds.

entries.clue: Liverpool’s Mo snubbed: flipping shame (4)

annotation.definitionNote: Both are cries rather than nouns here: 'Shame!' is what people say, and the answer is the older word for saying it.

indicatorNotes.snubbed: To snub someone is to cut them short, and a name cut short loses the letter it ends on.
indicatorNotes.flipping: Something flipped comes to rest the other way about, so those letters are read from the back.

blocks.note: Mohamed Salah, the Egyptian forward who has played for Liverpool FC since 2017
the H at the end comes away, leaving four letters

annotation.surface: Liverpool's Mo Salah being cut dead, which is a crying shame.
annotation.walkthrough: The footballer is named by club and first name only, which is how the back pages refer to him. 'Flipping' is a mild English swear word in the surface and a turnaround instruction in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Alas is the old exclamation of regret, and 'what a shame' is how the same feeling is said now, so one stands in for the other.

entries.clue: US novelist’s hideous neck bites (9)

indicatorNotes.hideous: What is hideous is misshapen, and letters out of shape are letters out of order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Horrible bite marks on somebody's neck.
annotation.walkthrough: Bites on a neck point at horror films and the answer is a surname: John Steinbeck wrote The Grapes of Wrath and Of Mice and Men, and took the Nobel prize in 1962.
annotation.definitionFit: Steinbeck was an American novelist of the Depression years, so the surname alone answers to the description of him.

entries.clue: Dream job as described by croupier? (5)

blocks.note: the croupier is speaking of the work in the first person
handing out the cards is what a croupier is there to do

annotation.surface: The perfect post, described by the person who hands out the cards.
annotation.walkthrough: A croupier is the casino employee who deals the cards and rakes in the chips, and asked what the work involves would say 'I deal'. The question mark admits that the words are split in an unusual place.
annotation.definitionFit: A dream holiday or a dream job is the ideal one, so 'dream' used as an adjective is a straight swap for the answer.

entries.clue: Expresses disapproval, having a thing or two (7)

annotation.definitionNote: 'A thing or two' is the idiom for several things rather than exactly two, which is how a singular-sounding phrase defines a plural.

blocks.note: raises an objection out loud, as counsel does in court
things in the plainest sense, the items you can pick up and put down

annotation.surface: Somebody grumbling who clearly knows a thing or two.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Having a thing or two' sounds like the idiom for knowing your stuff, and it is a plain plural noun instead. The first half is the courtroom word, thrown in before a judge rules on it.
annotation.definitionFit: To object is to voice disapproval, and objects are simply things — one word, a verb in court and a noun on a shelf.

entries.clue: Egyptian kings heard in N Atlantic islands (7)

indicatorNotes.heard: What is heard is taken by ear, so the letters follow the sound of the words rather than their spelling.

blocks.note: the rulers of ancient Egypt were pharaohs, and the islands are spelt the way that word is said

annotation.surface: The pharaohs of Egypt getting a mention somewhere in the north Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: The Faeroes are eighteen islands between Scotland and Iceland, self-governing under the Danish crown. The plural matters: one king would leave the final letter of the answer unpaid for.
annotation.definitionFit: The Faeroe Islands sit in the north Atlantic between Shetland and Iceland, so the definition places them rather than describing them.

entries.clue: Predicts California surrounded by trees (9)

indicatorNotes.surrounded by: What is surrounded has something closed round it, so the short piece is planted inside the longer word rather than joined on.

blocks.note: trees in quantity make forests, and this word opens up after its fourth letter
ca is the two-letter postal abbreviation for the state

annotation.surface: California hemmed in on every side by forest.
annotation.walkthrough: CA is California's postal code, familiar from any US address. 'Surrounded by trees' reads as scenery and works as an instruction to open the trees up and set the state inside them.
annotation.definitionFit: A forecast predicts what is coming — weather, sales, election results — and the verb takes the same third-person -s as 'predicts'.

entries.clue: Shunning middle speed – cam faulty – makes off at speed (7)

indicatorNotes.Shunning middle: To shun the middle is to leave it out, so the central letter of the following word is dropped before anything else happens.
indicatorNotes.faulty: Something faulty is not working as it should, so the letters gathered so far will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: the middle letter of the five is shunned, leaving four
three more letters for the fodder, the lobe on a rotating shaft
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A speed camera that has stopped working properly.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter uses the same word twice, once as fodder and once inside the definition, and the dashes are there to keep the speed camera in one piece across the middle of the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: To decamp is to pack up and leave in a hurry, originally to strike camp and march off, so it is a departure made fast and without ceremony.

entries.clue: Morning: judo master drinks whiskey (4)

indicatorNotes.drinks: What a drinker takes in goes inside them, so the single letter is swallowed by the word in front.

blocks.note: a dan is a black-belt grade in judo, counted upward from first dan
w is whiskey in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: A judo black belt taking a drink first thing in the morning.
annotation.walkthrough: Judo grades its black belts in dans, so a master of the sport is one. The spelling of the drink is the tell: whiskey with an e is the signaller's letter, not the Scotch.
annotation.definitionFit: Dawn is first light, the opening of the morning, so the two name the same part of the day — one the moment, one the stretch that follows it.

entries.clue: Tennis champ, twitching newcomer taking week off (7)

indicatorNotes.twitching: A twitch is an involuntary jerk, and letters that will not sit still do not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.taking week off: Taking something off removes it, so the letter standing for week leaves the word before the rest are rearranged.

blocks.note: the word with its w taken off, seven letters left for the fodder
w is the everyday short form of week, and this is the letter taken off
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A jumpy new player who has taken a week's holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: John McEnroe won Wimbledon three times and the US Open four, and was famous for shouting at umpires. 'Twitching' sits next to a person rather than next to a word, which is what hides the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: McEnroe took seven singles grand slams in the late seventies and early eighties, so 'tennis champ' names him by the game he dominated.

entries.clue: Stops when Democrat becomes Republican and fights (7)

indicatorNotes.becomes: One thing becoming another replaces it, so the letter standing for the first party is lifted out and the letter for the second put in its place.

blocks.note: to desist is to stop what you are doing
d is the letter printed after a Democrat's name in US election coverage
r is the matching letter for a Republican, and it takes the other's place

annotation.surface: A Democrat crossing the floor to the Republicans and then squaring up for a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: American results put a D or an R after every name on the ballot, which is what makes the swap readable. The definition is the last word, so the sentence runs its wordplay first and hides the seam behind 'and'.
annotation.definitionFit: To resist is to fight back against something pressing on you, so 'fights' catches the sense of putting up opposition rather than starting the trouble.

entries.clue: Son competed, spread out (7)

blocks.note: s is the family-tree abbreviation for son
to play a match is to compete in it, here in the past tense

annotation.surface: A son who took part in a game and afterwards sprawled.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits where a third verb in the story should be, so the comma reads as punctuation in a list. Splayed fingers or splayed feet are turned outward away from each other.
annotation.definitionFit: Something splayed has been spread wide apart — fingers, feet, the legs of a ladder — so the word and 'spread out' describe the same shape.

entries.clue: Agricultural servant to get on board, you say? (4)

indicatorNotes.you say: 'You say' points at the sound of the words, so what reaches the grid is the spelling that matches the ear rather than the page.

blocks.note: to get on a board and ride a wave is to surf, and the answer is that word as the ear takes it

annotation.surface: A farm labourer taking up surfing.
annotation.walkthrough: The board is a surfboard and not a committee — 'get on board' is the business cliché the question mark quietly withdraws. A serf was a peasant bound to his lord's land under the feudal system.
annotation.definitionFit: A serf was tied to the land and worked it without wages, which is servitude in agriculture rather than in a household.

entries.clue: Consume in haste – the result? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half defines by proverb rather than by synonym: haste makes waste, so 'the result' of hurry is the noun the answer supplies.

blocks.note: to use a thing up to no purpose, the sense in which fuel or a whole afternoon goes for nothing
the proverb says what hurry produces, and the question mark is the setter asking you to finish it

annotation.surface: Bolting your food down, and what comes of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Haste makes waste' is the proverb the second half leans on, so the question mark stands in for 'what you get'. The first half wants the verb in 'wasted resources', not the noun in the bin.
annotation.definitionFit: To waste something is to consume it to no purpose, and the proverb makes it exactly what hurry leaves behind.

entries.clue: Flight in which you might be still moving? (9)

annotation.definition: Flight in which you might be still moving?

blocks.note: read as an aeroplane journey, and meant as a flight of steps

blocks.clueFragment: in which you might be still moving?
blocks.note: the paradox is the point: a passenger stands perfectly still and is carried upward all the same

annotation.surface: A plane journey on which the passengers can be sitting still and travelling at once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the hinge, meaning motionless in one reading and yet in the other, and only the first gets you the machine. Moving stairs were patented as an amusement ride at Coney Island before they reached the shops.
annotation.definitionFit: An escalator is a staircase that carries you, so it is a flight of steps on which standing still and going up are the same thing.

entries.clue: Everyman’s ultimately prizeless after Everyman’s up for awards (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: What comes ultimately comes last of all, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is taken.
indicatorNotes.after: What goes after something follows it, so the letters named first in the clue are put at the back.
indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry the grid is climbed, so the letters named arrive the opposite way round from how they are said.

blocks.note: the setter signs himself Everyman, so what is his is ME, and climbing the column those two letters arrive this way round
what belongs to Everyman is his own, written in the first person
the closing letter of the word the instruction points at

annotation.surface: Everyman goes home empty-handed on a night when he was nominated.
annotation.walkthrough: The Emmys are American television's annual prizes, the small screen's Oscars. Everyman is the setter's own signature, and it does two jobs in one sentence: his word for himself, then the same word turned round.
annotation.definitionFit: The Emmys are handed out each year for American television, so the plural name is a set of awards and nothing else.

entries.clue: Poem Iris edited before the reader, Scout’s Honour (1,7,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a set phrase rather than a synonym: 'Scout's honour' is what somebody says to swear a thing is true, which is the undertaking the answer gives.

indicatorNotes.edited: An editor moves words about, so the letters named do not stay in the order they arrived in.
indicatorNotes.before: What comes before the rest goes in front, so the rearranged letters lead and the reader is left to follow.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
the person reading the clue is you
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A poem of Iris's, worked over before it reaches the reader, sworn to on Scout's honour.
annotation.walkthrough: Scout's honour is the promise made with three fingers raised, which is why it can stand for a spoken guarantee. The italics mark it as something said aloud rather than described.
annotation.definitionFit: A Scout swears on his honour that what he has said is true, which is the same assurance the answer offers the person hearing it.

entries.clue: Heathen siege surrounds classical city (6)

indicatorNotes.surrounds: What surrounds a thing sits on both sides of it, so the two words have closed round an unbroken run of letters.

blocks.note: the run begins three letters into the first word and finishes on the head of the second

annotation.surface: A pagan army camped outside the walls of an ancient city.
annotation.walkthrough: The run straddles the gap between two words, which is where a hidden answer is hardest to see. 'Classical' means the Greek and Roman world, so the definition dates the city rather than placing it.
annotation.definitionFit: Athens was the leading city of classical Greece — the Parthenon, Socrates, the first democracy — so the era alone identifies it.

entries.clue: Eased a temper? Only somewhat calm (6)

indicatorNotes.Only somewhat: Only somewhat means not the whole of it, so what is wanted is part of the words as they stand and not all of them.

blocks.note: the run starts two letters into the first word and stops two letters into the last

annotation.surface: Somebody's temper has been only partly soothed.
annotation.walkthrough: The run crosses two word breaks, and the question mark holds the surface together while it does. As an adjective the answer means unhurried and composed, the state the doctor's verb produces.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone sedate is calm and unruffled in manner, the quiet adjective that sits behind the drug named for producing it.
